taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes certain populations were formerly called Tantilla planiceps or T. utahensis (Cole and Hardy 1981 revision); Animal Diversity Web and BLM list it as 'southwestern blackhead snake'.
fieldMarks: Small, slender snake, uniformly brown above with a black head and a cream or white collar.
Belly has a broad reddish stripe down the centre of the ventral scales.
Secretive, semi-fossorial: usually seen only under cover or moving at night.
behavior: Secretive and difficult to detect except under specific temperature, moisture and time conditions; found under loose boards, logs, wood, rocks and fallen shrubs.
Probably nocturnal; active about April to October in the north and from early March in Texas.
Eats insect larvae (beetles, caterpillars), centipedes and millipedes.
Known clutches have held a single large egg, laid June-August.
habitat: Pinyon-juniper, chaparral-woodland, riparian woodland, mesquite-yucca grassland, sagebrush-greasewood and other arid scrub with friable sandy or organic soil and surface debris; prefers moist niches in arid country.
range: Discontinuous from southern California, southern Nevada, Utah and west-central Colorado south to Arizona, southern New Mexico and Texas, and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Western black-headed snake (Tantilla planiceps)
lookalikes.howToTell: Visually similar; separated mainly by range, as T. planiceps is now the California and Baja California species while populations east of California belong to T. hobartsmithi.
